The instruction is simple: a thousand words, write whatever comes to you. But the blank page has a way of making simplicity feel like a dare. The cursor blinks, patient and indifferent, a tiny metronome counting out the silence. I could start anywhere. I could start with the weather, with the way the afternoon light is leaning against the window, with the sound of a truck shifting gears somewhere down the street. I could start with a memory, a dream, a half-remembered line from a poem. The problem is not having nothing to say; it is having too much, and knowing that most of it will be forgotten the moment the next thought arrives.

Language is strange that way. We carry around this enormous machinery of words, millions of possible combinations, and yet when asked to simply produce, we often freeze. It is like being in a room with a thousand doors and no walls. Every sentence is a choice, and every choice closes off some other path. Maybe that is why so much writing is about looking backward—we are trying to understand why we chose the doors we did, why we are standing in this particular room, why the walls appeared at all.

I think about the word "whatever." It is a shrug made of letters. It can mean "I don't care" or "anything is fine" or "I have given up"—but it can also mean "everything is welcome." The instruction says write whatever comes to you, so I will try to honor that. I will try not to shape, not to polish, not to worry about whether this is good or coherent or worth reading. I will just let the current carry me.

Right now, the current is carrying me toward a kitchen. I am eight years old, sitting at a yellow table, eating cereal that has gone soggy because I was reading the back of the box. The box has a puzzle on it, a maze, and I am tracing the path with my finger. My mother is washing dishes, humming something I cannot name. The sun is falling through the window in a long rectangle, and dust motes are drifting through it like tiny planets. That moment is gone, of course, but here it is again, summoned by no particular need. Memory is a haunted house where every room is still lit.

I wonder if that is what writing is for: not to preserve the past, but to let it visit the present. When I write about that kitchen, I am not really recounting a fact. I am building a small shrine to a feeling—the feeling of being safe, of having no responsibilities, of believing that the world is mostly okay. And the strange thing is that the feeling is not in the memory itself. It is in the space between the words. The yellow table, the soggy cereal, the dust motes—they are just props. The real thing is the glow around them, the way memory bends light.

But I do not want to be sentimental. The past is not always a warm room. There are other memories, darker ones, that I could summon if I let myself. There are moments I have spent years trying not to look at directly. There are words I said that I would like to unsay, words said to me that still sting like broken glass. The page does not care which of these I choose. It will hold whatever I spill. That is both the beauty and the terror of writing: it is a place where we can be honest, but honesty is not always comfortable.

Maybe that is why so many of us avoid it. We say we do not have time, or we are not writers, or we do not know where to start. But the real reason might be that we are afraid of what will surface. The mind is not a clean filing cabinet; it is a swamp. Put your hand in, and you never know what you will pull out—a flower, a fish, an old boot, a wedding ring. The instruction "write whatever comes to you" is an invitation to wade into that swamp without a map.

I am trying to do that now. I am thinking about the concept of "now," actually. By the time I type this word, the moment I was thinking about has already passed. Language is always a step behind life. We cannot write the present; we can only write the immediate past, the afterimage. And yet we pretend otherwise. We speak as if we are capturing things, but we are only tracing outlines. The bird is gone; the shadow remains.

There is a name for this, I think, in some philosophy or another—the gap between the real and the represented. But I do not need a name. I can feel it in every sentence. I can feel it in this sentence. The words are not the thing; they are only pointers, arrows made of breath and ink, pointing toward something that cannot be held. And maybe that is enough. Maybe pointing is all we can do. Maybe the whole of human literature is just a massive collection of arrows, all pointing in slightly different directions, all trying to describe the same unreachable center.

What is at the center? I do not know. Perhaps it is simply the awareness that we are alive, that we are here, that we are conscious and temporary and full of contradictions. We are the only animals who tell stories about themselves, who make up reasons for our own behavior, who can imagine futures that will never happen and pasts that never did. We are strange, and the strangeness is worth recording.

I think of all the words I have written in my life—homework assignments, love letters, angry notes, grocery lists, text messages, essays like this one. They are scattered across time like confetti after a parade. Most of them mean nothing now. A few mean everything. The love letters are probably in a shoebox somewhere, or in a landfill, or burned to ash. The grocery lists are definitely gone. But the act of writing them mattered. It shaped me. Every word I have ever written was a small decision, and those decisions added up to a life.

The same is true of reading. Every book I have ever read is in me somewhere, like sediment in a riverbed. I can never fully separate my own thoughts from those I have borrowed from others. That sentence sounds like someone else. This sentence sounds like me. But what is "me" anyway? A bundle of influences, a patchwork of quotations, a voice that only exists because other voices existed first. We are all collages. We are all covers of songs we half-remember.

This is what comes to me: the awareness that I am not alone in this room, even though I am alone. The writers I have loved are here, in the rhythm of my sentences. The people I have known are here, in the shape of my concerns. The language itself is here, older than all of us, carrying the weight of everyone who has ever spoken it. When I write, I am not an individual; I am a temporary conduit for a river that has been flowing for thousands of years.

I am nearing the end now. I can feel the word count approaching, like a shore after a long swim. The instruction was a thousand words, and I have almost reached it. There is a temptation to end with something profound, a final chord that makes the whole piece feel intentional. But that would be a lie. This is not intentional. This is just what came to me.

So I will end without a flourish. I will end with the image of the cursor, still blinking, waiting for the next instruction. I will end with the yellow table and the dust motes, with the gap between the real and the represented, with the arrow pointing at the center that cannot be named. I will end with thank you—to the words, to the moment, to whatever force made it possible for any of us to be here, wondering, typing, alive. And then, since every ending is also a beginning, I will take a breath. And I will be quiet.
